thesis: The same venue simultaneously prices a 55% chance the Fed hikes again in October and 66% by December, and only a 22-23% chance the economy contracts for two consecutive quarters at any point across a five-quarter window. Those are hard to hold together: the hiking is happening because CPI ran +0.40% month-over-month in August (annualizing near 4.9%), and the fetched Fed funds effective rate already moved 3.63% to 3.88% in September. Policy tightening into an already-soft consumer is the standard route to two negative quarters, and the equity tape is voting — NKE, CCL, KBH and KMX all closed below both their 20- and 50-day averages with NKE and CCL sitting within 0.2% of their 120-day lows. Crucially the contract resolves on BEA advance estimates, not an NBER committee call, so the usual objection that a recession is dated years in arrears does not apply here — and the technical two-quarter bar is lower than an NBER recession, which 2022 cleared without NBER ever declaring one.
key_risk: The window is generous but the definition is strict: real GDP has printed two consecutive negative quarters only a handful of times in forty years, and a hiking Fed has repeatedly engineered slowdowns that stopped short of it. Capital is tied up for up to 17 months for a binary that pays nothing until it resolves, and a 23c position can drift to 10c for a year before any of this is settled. Answered, partly: that is precisely why the market prices further hikes, and it is the second and third hike from here, not the first, that turns real rates positive. It is a genuine reason to size this at 1.5% rather than larger, and to treat 35% as an estimate with wide error bars rather than a conviction-5 claim.
